name: Brennan Center for Justice (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: everyone the work reaches (US democracy, US prisons and jails) is in the United States.
summary: The Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan law and policy institute in New York and Washington, spent $57.6 million in the year to June 2025 on research, litigation and advocacy for voting rights and fair elections, checks on presidential power, and ending mass incarceration. Its democracy work (88% of the cost) is counted as its 1.1% share of the whole US pro-democracy field's yearly cut in the chance that US democracy breaks down before 2030 (a 15% chance, cut by a twentieth), valued by the income a breakdown would cost; its justice work as its 1.1% share of the reform field's part in the national decline in incarceration, valued by prisoners' wellbeing and shortened lives. It comes to about 0.003 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, far below the site's global-health median because a breakdown's income loss builds up over decades while an averted one counts only the five years the site counts a won change (a tenth of the loss on average), and because the Center holds about two years of spending in liquid reserves, so its next dollar counts at 32% of the average. The result is mostly uncertainty (the field's effect on the risk and the years counted; the model's own ranges alone span over ten thousandfold), and both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: Long-run income gain from staying a democracy (share of GDP per person)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Acemoglu et al. 2019): about a fifth of income per person, what a lasting fall out of democracy would cost in the long run.

rows.label: Share of that gain a US breakdown would lose
rows.explainer: A fall to what the Economist Intelligence Unit calls a hybrid regime would count as a transition out of democracy in Acemoglu et al.'s coding, but the US would keep parts of what drives the gain (independent states, courts, a free economy) and could recover within the years counted. Half the long-run gain, from a fifth to all of it; no study measures it for a rich country.

rows.label: Average share of the loss reached over the years counted
rows.explainer: The income effect builds up over about 25 years (@democracy.democratization_years_to_effect), taken as linear: over the 5 years counted ($win_years_counted) the loss averted averages a tenth of its long-run size; at 25 years or more, the average of the build-up and the full effect after it.

rows.label: Income loss averted per person per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + gain × severity × build-up): the shared log scale for income, valued at $uov_per_ln_consumption in the bridge.

rows.label: Chance the US stops being a democracy before 2030

source.title: Manifold, Will the Economist Intelligent Unit stop classifying the United States as a democracy before 2030?
source.quote: Will the Economist Intelligent Unit stop classifying the United States as a democracy before 2030?
source.note: 11% on 14 November 2026; resolves yes if any EIU Democracy Index report published before 1 January 2030 classes the US as a hybrid or authoritarian regime. V-Dem's Democracy Report 2026 (https://www.v-dem.net/documents/75/V-Dem_Institute_Democracy_Report_2026_lowres.pdf, p. 33: 'Within one year, the USA's LDI score has declined by 24%') downgraded the US from liberal to electoral democracy and notes that 'Electoral components of democracy remain stable.' Range: our judgment, 5% (the market's long-dated questions are thought to underprice change) to 35% (the experts V-Dem cites who call the regime already authoritarian).

rows.explainer: The risk the work reduces: 15% (5% to 35%), above the 11% a forecasting market gives for the Economist Intelligence Unit downgrading the US to a hybrid regime before 2030, because V-Dem recorded the steepest one-year fall in US democracy it has measured (2025) and a market long-dated question tends to sit near no change. Not a single event drawn as happens or not: the model counts the change in its chance, as the catastrophic-risk models count a cut in a hazard.

rows.label: Relative cut in that chance from one year of the whole US pro-democracy field's work
rows.explainer: What a year of the field's litigation, election-administration support, research and advocacy (about $4.5 billion, below) takes off the chance of a breakdown: a twentieth of it (1% to 20%). Anchors: in 2025 courts blocked most of the March 2025 elections executive order and the Justice Department's demands for state voter files in suits the field brought (Brennan Center 2025 annual report), and V-Dem finds the electoral components the field defends still stable while the others fell; against that, Baumgartner et al. found the side with more money hardly likelier to win (@democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate), and most of what decides a breakdown (voters, officials, courts, the parties) is outside the field. The biggest uncertainty in the model.

rows.label: Chance a year of the field's work averts a breakdown
rows.explainer: Breakdown risk × the field's relative cut; the Brennan Center's share of the field is in dem_attribution_share.

rows.label: Years from the work until it protects an election
rows.explainer: A year's work protects the next federal elections (November 2026, then 2028): about a year after the year modelled (0 to 2).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years a breakdown averted counts
rows.explainer: The years counted ($win_years_counted), with the shared yearly chance that a protected arrangement is undone anyway (@democracy.electoral_reform_repeal_rate) beside the discount rate (families/rights-advocacy.md, Democracy and governance).

source.title: Democracy Fund, Field in Focus: The State of Pro-Democracy Institutional Philanthropy (October 2023)
source.quote: By our estimate, institutional philanthropy is currently investing an average of $2.7 to $3.4 billion a year to support democracy.

rows.explainer: Institutional philanthropy gave $2.7 to $3.4 billion a year in 2021-2022 (Democracy Fund); individual donors (most of the Brennan Center's own contributions) and the growth since (funders' new pledges after 2024) come on top: $4.5 billion, from $3 billion (the institutional figure alone) to $7 billion. The field is the same one whose cut in risk is dem_field_cut, so a wider definition lowers the share and raises the cut together.

rows.label: The Brennan Center's share of the field's resources
rows.explainer: Its democracy cost over the field's spending (Convention 2): about 1.1%. Its donated legal services ($2.8 million) are other resources inside the field's total.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment for the democracy branch
rows.explainer: The income effect is a cross-country panel of mostly poorer countries applied to the US (external validity), and the risk is a market forecast; 0.5, from 0.25 to 0.8, lower than IRAP's advocacy model (0.8), whose value of a move rests on measured consumption.

rows.label: Share of the democracy outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: dem_field_cut is already the change against no field (what would have happened anyway is the rest of the breakdown chance), so it isn't asked twice (Convention 5).

rows.label: Share of the democracy outcome enforced
rows.explainer: 1: the cut is in the chance of the outcome itself, after whether rulings are obeyed.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, democracy branch
rows.explainer: Thin: no measure of the Brennan Center's effect on US democracy exists; the branch rests on the literature and judgment, so it takes the shared missing-data step (Convention 12).

People per year newly kept out of prison or jail by the US decline in incarceration

source.title: Bureau of Justice Statistics, Correctional Populations in the United States, 2022 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 308699), table 1

rows.explainer: The yearly flow of the decline (Convention 3): 2,231,300 people incarcerated in 2012 and 2,086,000 in 2019 (table 1, the same column: '2019 6,343,300 4,357,700 3,492,900 878,900 2,086,000'), 145,300 fewer over seven years, 20,757 a year. High: the 2012-2022 average (403,700 fewer, 40,370 a year), inflated by the pandemic's releases. Low: the decline has stalled since (the incarcerated population rose 2.9% in 2022), so the field's yearly gain may now be near 5,000.

rows.label: Share of the decline caused by policy changes (sentencing, bail, parole, drug laws)
rows.explainer: Over 2012-2019 crime fell little while states passed justice-reinvestment, sentencing and bail laws and the federal First Step Act (2018); the rest is falling arrests and admissions for other reasons. 60%, from 30% to 85%: no study apportions the national decline.

rows.label: Share of those policy changes owed to the reform advocacy field
rows.explainer: Against officials, budgets, courts and prosecutors elected on reform: the advocacy field (research, campaigns, coalitions across left and right) is credited with 40%, from 15% to 70%, a judgment like IRAP's advocacy model's share of the refugee programme's rebuild owed to advocacy.

rows.label: Share of each year's decline the reform field caused
Wellbeing gained per year out of prison (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Dutch prisoners rated their happiness 6.59 and controls 7.36 on a 0-10 scale (0.77 points), and their mood through the day 5.25 against 6.73 (1.48; Pappot and Phaff 2004, World Database of Happiness, https://worlddatabaseofhappiness.eur.nl/studies/pappot-phaff-2004-study-nl-2004-1010, N = 42); a US study found a much larger gap (Chason 1975: 1.23 against 2.22 on a 1-3 scale). US prisons are harsher than Dutch ones: 1 point, from 0.5 to 2.5.

rows.label: Years of life lost per year in prison

source.title: Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.quote: each additional year in prison produced a 15.6% increase in the odds of death for parolees, which translated to a 2-year decline in life expectancy for each year served in prison

rows.explainer: New York parolees, 1989-2003: 2 years of life per year served. Observational, with longer sentences going to people at higher risk anyway, so the low end is a quarter of it (0.5); high 3.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person in prison
rows.explainer: People in US prisons are mostly in their thirties and forties, with life expectancy below the general population's: 40 years left (33 to 47). Turns years of life lost into a share of a death.

rows.label: Value of a death averted at prison ages
rows.explainer: The shared value of a death at ages 15-49 (most people in prison), times the shared multiplier.

rows.label: Deaths averted per year out of prison
rows.explainer: Years of life lost over the years left: about a twentieth of a death per year in prison.

rows.label: Years from the work until the reforms reduce incarceration
rows.explainer: Laws and rules take effect within months to a few years of passing, and sentences shorten as cases come through: 1 year (0 to 3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years a reduction counts
rows.explainer: A reduction in incarceration is a won reform: it counts $win_years_counted years, discounted; rollbacks are a side effect below.
